hints: Notice the contrast in the question between most alpha-particles passing through the gold foil undeflected and a tiny proportion deflected through large angles.
Recall that a large-angle deflection of a massive $+2e$ alpha-particle needs a very large repulsive force from a concentrated positive charge.
Ask which observation the plum-pudding model of spread-out positive charge cannot explain but a tiny dense nucleus can explain.
walkthrough: Recall the set-up: alpha-particles fired at thin gold foil, with most passing straight through and only very few scattered.
State the governing physics: deflection is caused by electrostatic repulsion between the positive alpha-particle and positive charge in the atom.
Argue that a spread-out charge, as in the plum-pudding model, can only produce weak forces and small deflections.
Conclude that deflection through a large angle, even back-scattering, needs a close approach to a tiny region holding almost all the mass and positive charge.
That rare large-angle scattering is therefore direct evidence for the nucleus. This is option A.

options.A: Most alpha-particles pass straight through, but rare large-angle scattering requires a tiny, dense, highly charged centre to repel them strongly.
options.B: Slower particles spending longer near the foil are deflected more, but this shows details of Coulomb repulsion, not the existence of the nucleus itself.
options.C: Unchanged kinetic energy shows the scattering is elastic, not that all the positive charge is concentrated in a nucleus.
options.D: Dependence on foil thickness shows more atoms give more scattering chances, not that each atom has a small central nucleus.
